prompt.context: A pharmaceutical company is developing a therapy for lymphoma. The CEO came to you for help in designing the clinical trial.
prompt.question: How should you proceed in designing the clinical trial?

clarifying_info.q: Are there different types of lymphoma?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — 75% non-Hodgkin lymphoma and 25% Hodgkin lymphoma.

clarifying_info.q: What are the different stages of lymphoma?
clarifying_info.a: Localized, Regional, Distant, and Unknown — see Exhibit 1 for survival rates and case distribution.
Total cases in the US are approximately 700,000; new cases increase by approximately 10% per year.
Lymphoma is the most common type of cancer in developed countries.
There is no treatment, only management therapies to alleviate symptoms using radiotherapy and chemotherapy. These are not specific to lymphoma and risks and harm outweigh the benefits.

clarifying_info.q: Is the client's therapy for management or treatment?
clarifying_info.a: It is a non-aggressive management therapy intended for both types of lymphoma.

clarifying_info.q: Has the therapy shown promising results for both types of lymphoma?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — low risks and safe results shown in animal studies for both types.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's funding situation?
clarifying_info.a: The client has sufficient funds to run multiple trials.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current prognosis of this disease?
clarifying_info.a: The five-year survival rate varies by stage — see Exhibit 1. Distant-stage patients have the lowest five-year survival rate at 60%.

exhibits.title: Lymphoma Stage at Diagnosis: Survival and Case Distribution
exhibits.shows: A table showing four stages of lymphoma diagnosis (Localized, Regional, Distant, Unknown), each with a corresponding five-year survival rate (%) and percentage of total cases (%).

framework: Lymphoma disease space — types and stages of lymphoma, epidemiology, existing therapies and their pros/cons
Client's therapy — whether it is treatment or management, which indication(s) it targets, safety profile
Indication selection — which type (Hodgkin vs. non-Hodgkin) and which stage to target first
Clinical trial location and phases — US or other countries, Phase I safety, Phase II efficacy, Phase III confirmation, Phase IV post-marketing
End point measurement — define the primary endpoint (e.g., five-year survival rate)

questions.prompt: What is the total addressable patient population, and how is it distributed across lymphoma types?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note ~700,000 total US cases growing ~10%/year. 75% (~525,000) are non-Hodgkin and 25% (~175,000) are Hodgkin. Non-Hodgkin represents a larger and commercially more attractive population.

math.setup: Total US cases = 700,000; non-Hodgkin share = 75%; Hodgkin share = 25%.
steps: New cases per year ≈ 700,000 × 10% = 70,000 incremental patients annually
math.answer: ~525,000 non-Hodgkin and ~175,000 Hodgkin patients in the US; ~70,000 new cases per year.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, which stage should the clinical trial target, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify Distant stage as the priority target: it represents the largest share of cases (45%) and has the lowest five-year survival rate (60%), making it easiest to demonstrate efficacy improvement. The unmet need is highest in this group.

math.setup: Total US non-Hodgkin cases ≈ 525,000; Distant stage = 45% of all cases.
steps: Five-year survival rate for Distant stage = 60% (lowest among all stages)
math.answer: Distant-stage patients represent ~236,250 non-Hodgkin patients with the lowest survival rate (60%), giving the greatest statistical power to detect efficacy improvement.

questions.prompt: Where should the trial be conducted, and which indication should be pursued first?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates recommend starting in the US (largest patient pool, growing) and targeting non-Hodgkin lymphoma first (75% of cases). Clinical trials cost roughly $2B per drug to develop; starting with one indication is more capital-efficient. After Phase II success, the second indication (Hodgkin) can be added.

questions.prompt: Describe the four phases of a clinical trial and the appropriate end point for this therapy.
questions.guidance: Phase I — safety (dosage, frequency, clearance, side effects); Phase II — efficacy (five-year survival rate in Distant-stage patients); Phase III — final confirmation on safety and efficacy (large, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled); Phase IV — post-marketing surveillance. The five-year survival rate is the appropriate primary end point given that it is the standard prognostic measure for lymphoma and the Distant-stage population provides a low baseline (60%) where improvement is measurable.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional factors should the client consider when designing and executing the clinical trial?

categories.name: Patient recruitment
ideas: Partnering with oncology centers that see high lymphoma volume
Targeting geographies with high lymphoma prevalence
Considering patient advocacy groups for outreach
Setting inclusion/exclusion criteria to control for comorbidities

categories.name: Regulatory and approval
ideas: Engaging FDA early via pre-IND meetings
Exploring Breakthrough Therapy Designation given unmet need
Designing trial to meet FDA endpoints for lymphoma
Planning for international regulatory filings post-US approval

categories.name: Trial design
ideas: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled design for Phase III
Adaptive trial design to allow early stopping for efficacy or futility
Choosing appropriate comparator arm (existing management therapies)

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Monitoring competitor pipelines for similar lymphoma therapies
Filing patents on the therapy before trial commencement
Assessing potential for first-mover advantage in non-Hodgkin indication

categories.name: Commercial preparation
ideas: Planning manufacturing scale-up in parallel with Phase III
Engaging payers early to understand reimbursement landscape
Building medical affairs team to support KOL engagement

recommendation: Start the clinical trial in the US targeting non-Hodgkin lymphoma patients (75% of all cases, ~525,000 patients) given the large and growing patient population
Recruit patients at the Distant stage (45% of cases, lowest five-year survival at 60%) to maximize statistical power to demonstrate efficacy improvement
Use the five-year survival rate as the primary endpoint; once Phase II confirms efficacy, consider expanding the trial to Hodgkin lymphoma as a second indication
risks: Clinical development costs approximately $2B per drug — failure at Phase III would be extremely costly
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is heterogeneous; the therapy may not work uniformly across subtypes
Regulatory pathway may be lengthy even with Breakthrough Therapy Designation
Competitors may enter the space with similar or superior therapies during the multi-year trial period
next_steps: Conduct pre-IND meeting with FDA to align on trial design and endpoints
Select trial sites across high-volume US oncology centers
File patent protection on the therapy formulation
Develop patient recruitment protocol targeting Distant-stage non-Hodgkin patients
Begin Phase I safety study to confirm dosage and side-effect profile in humans
